glossary.Lymphocytes: White cells of the adaptive immune system: B cells and T cells.
glossary.Lymphatic system: The network of lymph vessels, nodes, spleen and thymus that drains tissue fluid and hosts immune cells.
glossary.Lymph nodes: Small bean-shaped immune organs along lymph vessels where lymphocytes gather.
glossary.Night sweats: Drenching sweats at night that soak clothes or sheets.
glossary.Systemic disease: Disease affecting the whole body rather than one place.
glossary.Prognosis: The likely course and outcome of a disease.
glossary.Bilobed nuclei: A nucleus with two lobes, giving Reed-Sternberg cells an 'owl's eye' look.
glossary.Eosinophilic nucleoli: Pink-staining nucleoli, prominent in Reed-Sternberg cells.
glossary.Nucleoli: Dense spots in the nucleus where ribosomes are made.
glossary.Mitotic rate: How many cells are dividing; high in aggressive tumours.
glossary.Immunosuppression: A weakened immune system from disease or drugs.
glossary.HIV: Human immunodeficiency virus, which destroys CD4 T cells and raises lymphoma risk.
glossary.Mediastinal: In the central chest between the lungs.
glossary.Lymphoid organ: An organ of the immune system such as the spleen or thymus.
glossary.Diaphragm: The dome-shaped muscle separating chest from abdomen; staging counts which sides are involved.
glossary.Extra-lymphatic: Outside the lymph nodes and lymphatic organs.
glossary.Ultrasound: Imaging with sound waves, used to guide needle and node biopsy.
glossary.CT: Computed tomography: a cross-sectional X-ray scan.
glossary.FBC: Full blood count: haemoglobin, white cells and platelets.
glossary.Blood film: A stained smear of blood to look at cell shapes.
glossary.Watchful waiting: Monitoring without treatment until the disease progresses or causes symptoms.
glossary.Chemotherapy: Drugs that kill rapidly dividing cancer cells.
glossary.Radiotherapy: Treating cancer with targeted ionising radiation.
glossary.Hepatitis B: A liver virus that can flare dangerously when rituximab suppresses B cells.
glossary.Neutropenia: A low neutrophil count, leaving the patient open to severe infection.
glossary.Bone marrow suppression: Reduced blood cell production, a common side effect of chemotherapy.
glossary.Apoptosis: Programmed cell death that removes damaged or unwanted cells.
glossary.Apoptotic checkpoints: Controls that make faulty cells kill themselves.
glossary.Inflammatory infiltrate: A crowd of immune cells within a tissue.
glossary.Cytokines: Signalling proteins released by immune cells.
glossary.Catabolic: Breaking down body tissues for energy, causing weight loss.
glossary.Translocation: Swapping of pieces between two chromosomes.
glossary.Cell turnover: How fast cells divide and die.
glossary.Urate oxidase: An enzyme that converts uric acid to the more soluble allantoin.
glossary.Hyperuricaemia: High uric acid in the blood, which can crystallise in the kidneys.
glossary.Monoclonal antibody: A lab-made antibody that targets one specific molecule.
glossary.Complement-mediated lysis: Killing of a cell when complement proteins punch holes in its membrane.
glossary.B cells: Lymphocytes that make antibodies; most NHL comes from them.
glossary.Heterogeneous: Made up of many different types.
